families.name: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
families.definition: End-to-end trainable architectures, such as U-Net and its variants, that learn hierarchical features directly from raw image data for pixel-wise vessel classification.

properties.text: These methods utilize contracting and expanding paths to capture context and enable precise localization.
Variants incorporate attention gates, dilated convolutions, and multi-scale features to handle varying vessel sizes and global context.
3D CNNs are employed for volumetric data to account for spatial continuity across slices.
Deep supervision and residual connections are used to improve gradient flow and feature learning.
These networks can be trained with data augmentation to overcome the scarcity of annotated samples.

limitations.text: Standard pixel-wise losses often fail to capture the connectivity and structural integrity of thin vessels.
Class imbalance between vessel and background pixels limits the accuracy of thin vessel segmentation.
High computational complexity makes implementation difficult on portable diagnostic devices.
Methods often neglect the graphical structure of vessel shapes, relying solely on local appearances.
Performance degrades in the presence of pathologies like micro-aneurysms and hemorrhages that interfere with vessel contrast.

families.name: Graphical and Structured Prediction Models
families.definition: Methods that integrate graph neural networks, conditional random fields, or graph cuts to enforce topological constraints and connectivity during segmentation.

properties.text: Graph neural networks are incorporated into CNN architectures to jointly exploit local appearances and global vessel structures.
Fully connected conditional random fields use expressive potentials to handle thin and elongated structures better than standard priors.
Graph cut algorithms are used for segmentation and artery-vein classification by learning proximity features.
Structured learning frameworks integrate vascular filter responses into random forests for voxel classification.
These approaches model the relationship between vessel neighborhoods to improve segmentation accuracy.

limitations.text: Inference for fully connected models can be computationally intensive, though recent results allow near real-time processing.
Standard segmentation priors like Potts models or total variation fail when dealing with thin and elongated structures.
The methods require careful design of graph structures or potentials to effectively capture vessel connectivity.

families.name: Probabilistic and Tracking-Based Methods
families.definition: Algorithms that use probabilistic trackers, particle filters, or Bayesian approaches to estimate vessel geometry, centerlines, and connectivity.

properties.text: Sequential Monte Carlo tracking fuses multiple cues such as intensity, vesselness, and organ detection for vessel localization.
Gaussian processes are used to model vessel curvature and diameter for tracking and bifurcation detection.
Recursive Bayesian approaches couple deep network outputs with probabilistic trackers for parameter estimation.
Hierarchical probabilistic models classify local intensity cross-sections to identify junctions and vessel points.
These methods are effective for assessing connectivity and determining geometric relationships.

limitations.text: These methods are often semi-automated, requiring manual seed points or initial guidance.
They can be sensitive to noise and inhomogeneities in the imaging data.
The computational cost of particle filtering and Bayesian inference can be high for large volumes.

families.name: Feature-Based and Classical Machine Learning
families.definition: Techniques that rely on hand-crafted features, matched filters, or ensemble classifiers like Random Forests and AdaBoost for vessel detection.

properties.text: Matched filters and directionally sensitive enhancement are used to highlight vessel structures before classification.
Random forests and AdaBoost classifiers are trained on features such as Hessian eigenvalues and local self-similarity.
Texton-based methods use filter banks to identify texture features for vascular tree segmentation.
Supervised feature learning can learn discriminative convolutional filters in closed form.
These methods often combine low-level features with higher-level discriminative features for probability map generation.

limitations.text: Hand-crafted features require significant domain knowledge and parameter tuning.
These methods are often insufficiently validated compared to deep learning approaches.
They struggle with large intra-scale changes and inter-anatomy variations.
Performance is limited by the quality of the selected features and the classifier's ability to generalize.

families.name: Weakly-Supervised and Unsupervised Learning
families.definition: Frameworks that reduce the need for dense manual annotations by using knowledge transfer, generative models, or weak labels.

properties.text: Knowledge transfer from annotated retinal images is used to segment coronary arteries without direct annotation.
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) synthesize retinal and neuronal images to improve segmentation performance with small sample sizes.
Weakly-supervised learning iterates between multi-modal registration and learning to avoid de novo labeling.
Semi-supervised methods leverage a small amount of labeled data with a large amount of unlabeled data.
Annotation-free approaches use shape-consistent GANs to generate and segment synthetic data.

limitations.text: These methods often require additional data sources, such as concurrently captured angiography images or public datasets from other organs.
The quality of the synthesized or transferred knowledge may not perfectly match the target domain.
Semi-supervised methods still require some initial labeled data to bootstrap the learning process.
Accurate segmentation of thin vessels and micro-vessels remains challenging due to low contrast and class imbalance.
There is a lack of standardized evaluation methodologies and reference databases for many specific vessel segmentation tasks, such as coronary centerline extraction.
Manual annotation of vessel structures is time-consuming, subjective, and often infeasible for large-scale clinical studies.
Methods struggle to handle the variability in blood flow signal strength and inhomogeneities in volumetric data like MRA.
The integration of global connectivity constraints with local pixel-wise accuracy is still an active area of research.
Portable diagnostic devices face limitations in implementing complex deep learning models due to computational constraints.
Differentiating arteries from veins in CT images is difficult due to similar intensity distributions and the need for physiological context.
